plain.title: Explaining it to two different people

questions.q: “Your AI checks its own work and gets better each time it tries. But your slowest customers now wait three times longer. Your teammate says just limit it to three tries. Why is that a plaster, and what's really wrong?”
questions.a:
Limiting the tries doesn't fix the slowness. It hides it — by quietly giving up on the hardest jobs, where nobody is looking.

The real problem is that nothing in the system ever tastes the food. It has no way to know when the work is good enough, so it keeps going until something forces it to stop.

questions.q: Why does saying “We'll set the max to three and ship it.” lose you the room?
questions.a: That's the exact answer the question is designed to catch.

questions.q: Why does saying “Just add more servers.” lose you the room?
questions.a: Sometimes right, but it pays for the bug instead of fixing it — and the bill scales with the bug.

questions.q: Why does saying “p99 is only 1% of requests, who cares.” lose you the room?
questions.a: If a user makes twenty calls, they hit that 1% about a fifth of the time. In a long AI agent run, the worst case is the normal experience.

questions.q: Why does saying “The model says its output improved, so it improved.” lose you the room?
questions.a: A model grading its own work is the thing that's missing here, not the evidence that it's fine.

questions.q: Why does telling a story with no measurement in it lose you the room?
questions.a: “What's broken” needs evidence. Always name what you'd measure first.

questions.q: Why does making your teammate look stupid lose you the room?
questions.a: They're right that you need a limit. The question put a colleague in the room on purpose — it's testing whether you can disagree and still ship their change.
